title: Load a butane canister into a cassette burner: notch up, pushed home against the seal, lever locked
instruction: Load the new gas canister into the burner so that the burner is ready to light.
context: Cooks at buffet, omelet and catering stations (Cooks, Restaurant, O*NET 35-2014.00, about 1.4 million US workers) and servers at hot-pot and Korean barbecue tables (Waiters and Waitresses, 35-3031.00, about 2 million) swap the canisters of portable butane cassette burners during service. The canister only connects with the notch on its rim facing straight up into the inlet's guide; it then has to be pushed into the inlet against its seal and held there while the locking lever is moved across. A canister left with its notch turned, short of home or unlocked leaks or will not light. Here the canister lies on the table with its notch turned 35 degrees off the top, so it has to be turned in the hand on the way in, and one hand must hold it home while the other works the lever.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, on the table (x forward, y left). Cassette burner: black steel body 28.2 (x) by 35 (y) cm, 8 cm tall, 1.6 kg, on rubber feet, its centre at x 33, y 0, not fixed. Its canister compartment runs front to back along its right side, 10 cm wide, centred on y -12.5, with 2.5 cm walls and two steel rails on which a canister lies with its axis 4.5 cm above the table. At the back (face at x 42) is the gas inlet: a socket with a round 4.4 cm opening and a 2.4 cm guide slot at its top, and a spring plunger 0.9 cm inside it (1.5 N per mm, 4.5 mm travel). The locking lever is a steel bar that slides 4 cm toward -y across behind a loaded canister's base (its back face at x 24.5); an arm over the control panel carries its orange handle (1.2 x 1.5 x 4 cm, top 10 cm above the table) at x 21.1, y 0.25. It stays where it is put. Butane cassette canister, 250 g size: red steel, 6.6 cm across, 19 cm long, 0.36 kg, lying on its side on the table, centre at x 30, y -30, nozzle end away from the arms (+x), the notch lug on its rim (1 x 1 cm, standing 0.8 cm off the 4 cm mounting cup) turned 35 degrees from straight up toward the right (-y).
scoring: Measured with a ruler and a photo, along the compartment from the burner's centre line. 0 if the burner was at any point moved more than 3 cm or tipped more than 10 degrees, or the canister fell off the table. Otherwise the canister counts as on the rails when its axis is within 10 mm of the compartment's line, 6 mm of its height and 10 degrees of its direction. 1.0 if it is home (its centre 8.5 to 14 mm past the centre line, its base against or just past the locking bar) with its notch within 15 degrees of straight up and the lever at least 3.5 of its 4 cm across, all held for 1 s with the canister still (moving less than 1 mm); 0.75 if it was ever home with its notch up; 0.5 if its nozzle was ever in the inlet (centre 5 mm or more past the line, which the lug allows only through the guide slot); 0.25 if it was ever on the rails with its centre between 60 mm before and 16 mm past the line; else 0.
reset_notes: Slide the lever back, pull the canister out and lay it back on its marked outline with the notch turned 35 degrees to the right.
fidelity: Rigid boxes and cylinders at real size and mass. The canister's rim notch is a lug that must pass a slot in the inlet; the inlet's seal and magnet coupling are a spring plunger; the locking lever, which turns down on real burners, is a bar slid across. The compartment cover is left off and the contents are rigid. Light angular damping is added; no contact force cap.
